title: School Bus
summary: Danger zones and mirrors, safe loading and unloading, evacuations, railroad crossings, student behavior, ABS and other special situations for school bus drivers.

blocks.text: The danger zone is the area on all sides of the bus where children are most likely to be hit, by another vehicle or by their own bus. It can reach 30 feet in front of the bumper (the first 10 feet are the most dangerous), 10 feet out from each side, and 10 feet behind the rear bumper. The area to the left of the bus is always dangerous because of passing cars.

rows: Watch traffic, clearances and students at the sides and rear. Adjust to see 200 feet (about 4 bus lengths) behind, along the sides, and the rear tires touching the ground. Blind spots: just below and in front of each mirror, and behind the rear bumper, usually 50-150 feet and up to 400 feet depending on the bus.
Wide-angle view of the sides. Adjust to see the whole side of the bus up to the mirror mounts, the front of the rear tires touching the ground, and at least one lane on each side.

Show the front danger zone you cannot see directly, plus the sides near the front wheels and service door. Adjust to see from the front bumper at ground level to where direct vision starts (the views should overlap), both front tires on the ground, and the area from the front of the bus to the service door.
Watch students. Adjust so the top of the rear window is in the top of the mirror and you can see every student, including the heads of those right behind you.

blocks.text: Convex and crossover mirrors do not show true size and distance. The inside mirror has a blind spot directly behind the driver's seat and a large one that starts at the rear bumper and can reach 400 feet or more, so watch traffic there with your outside side mirrors.

More students are killed getting on or off a school bus each year than riding inside one. The school district sets official routes and stops; never move a stop without written approval from the right school district official. Follow your state and local laws for stops.

blocks.caption: School Bus Stop Ahead: warns other drivers that a bus may be stopped to load or unload children.

items: Approach slowly and check all mirrors continuously.
If equipped, turn on the alternating flashing amber lights at least 200 feet, or about 5-10 seconds, before the stop (or as state law requires).
Turn on the right turn signal about 100-300 feet, or about 3-5 seconds, before pulling over. Move as far right as possible.
Stop with the front bumper at least 10 feet from the waiting students. This makes them walk to the bus so you can see them better.
Put the transmission in Park, or in Neutral with the parking brake set if there is no Park.
Turn on the alternating red lights when traffic is a safe distance away, and make sure the stop arm is out.
Check that all traffic has stopped before fully opening the door and signaling students to come.
Students should wait in a designated spot facing the bus, and board only when you signal them.

Count students and make sure all board; if one is missing, ask the other students where they are. Have them board slowly, in single file, using the handrail. Use the dome light when loading in the dark.
Wait until everyone is seated and facing forward. Check all mirrors and make sure no one is running to catch the bus.
If you cannot account for a student outside, secure the bus, take the key, and check around and under the bus.
Loading at school: turn off the ignition, remove the key if you leave the driver's compartment, and position yourself to supervise.

blocks.text: To leave the stop: close the door, engage the transmission, release the parking brake, turn off the red lights, turn on the left signal, check all mirrors again, and let traffic clear.

items: Have students stay seated until told to exit, and count them as they leave.
Tell them to walk at least 10 feet from the side of the bus, to a spot where you can plainly see them.
If you miss a student's stop, do not back up. Follow local procedures.
At school, secure the bus, supervise as students leave, then walk through the bus to check for hiding or sleeping students and left-behind items.
Walk about 10 feet away from the side of the bus.
Walk to a spot at least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper, staying away from the front of the bus.
Stop at the right edge of the road, where the driver can see the student's feet.
Look in all directions, check that the red lights are still flashing, and wait for the driver's signal.
Cross in front of the bus, stop at its left edge, and look again for the driver's signal.
Check both directions and keep looking while crossing the rest of the road.
Dropped objects: tell students to leave anything they drop, move to safety outside the danger zones, and get your attention to retrieve it.
Handrail hang-ups: clothing, accessories or body parts can catch in the handrail or door. Watch every student leave and confirm they are safe before moving.

Post-trip: walk through and around the bus looking for left-behind items, sleeping students, open windows and doors, damage or vandalism, and mechanical problems, especially with mirror systems, flashing warning lamps and stop signal arms.

blocks.text: The first and most important step is to recognize the hazard. If time allows, call your dispatcher before deciding to evacuate. In general, students are safest and easiest to control on the bus, unless staying exposes them to unnecessary risk.

rows: Fire or threat of fire; bus stalled on or next to a railroad crossing; the bus's position may shift and add danger; a collision is about to happen; a hazmat spill requires a quick exit.
Staying on the bus, away from the material, may be safer unless a quick evacuation is needed.
At least 100 feet off the road, in the direction of oncoming traffic, away from debris if the bus is hit.
Upwind, at least 300 feet from the bus.
As far from the tracks as possible, toward any oncoming train.
A nearby ditch or culvert, lying face down with hands over heads, far enough that the bus cannot topple on them. Avoid flash flood areas.

blocks.text: Plan ahead: when possible, assign two older, responsible students to each emergency exit and another to lead students to the safe place. Explain the evacuation procedures and how to work the exits to all students, since helpers may not be aboard.

items: Decide whether evacuation is in the best interest of safety, and choose the best exits: front, rear or side doors, roof or windows.
Secure the bus: Park (or Neutral if there is no Park), parking brakes set, engine off, key removed, hazard lights on.
If time allows, tell dispatch the location, conditions and help needed. Leave the radio microphone or phone dangling out the driver's window if it works.
With no working radio, send a passing motorist or area resident for help; as a last resort, send two older, responsible students.
Order the evacuation. A student assistant leads the others to the nearest safe place.
Walk through the bus to make sure no one remains, and retrieve emergency equipment.
Join the students, account for everyone, protect the scene with warning devices, and prepare information for responders.

blocks.text: Do not move a student who may have a neck or spinal injury unless his or her life is in immediate danger.

A passive crossing has no traffic control device. You must still stop, but the decision to go rests entirely with you, so be especially careful. Active crossings have flashing red lights with or without bells, or flashing lights with bells and gates. The round, black-on-yellow advance warning sign and the RR pavement marking tell you a crossing is ahead: slow down, look and listen, and be ready to stop.

items: Approaching: slow down (shift to a lower gear in a manual bus) and test your brakes. Turn on hazard lights about 200 feet before the crossing, check traffic behind you, stay to the right if possible, and pick an escape route in case of brake failure.
Stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail. If there is a white stop line, keep the front of the bus behind it; if not, stop before the crossbuck.
Put the bus in Park (or Neutral with brakes held), turn off radios and noisy equipment, and silence the passengers.
Open the service door and driver's window, and look and listen for a train.
Check the crossing signals again before proceeding.
At a multiple-track crossing, stop only before the first set. When sure no train is coming on any track, cross them all without stopping.
Cross in a low gear and do not change gears on the tracks.
If the gate comes down after you have started across, keep going, even if it breaks the gate.
If the gate stays down after a train passes, do not drive around it. Call your dispatcher.
If a police officer is at the crossing, obey directions. If not, and you think the signal is malfunctioning, call your dispatcher for instructions.
Never cross unless you can see far enough down the track to know for certain no train is coming. Even when active signals show the tracks are clear, look and listen.
If the bus stalls or is trapped on the tracks, get everyone off at once and move them far away at an angle that is away from the tracks and toward the train.
Containment space: you need the length of the bus plus 15 feet beyond the tracks. If it won't fit, don't commit.
Loading and unloading need your full attention. If a problem starts, wait until unloading students are off and away, then pull over if needed.
For serious problems, stop in a safe place off the road, secure the bus, and speak to the student calmly and firmly. Move the student to a seat near you if needed.
Never put a student off the bus except at school or at the student's own stop. If you cannot drive safely, call a school administrator or the police to remove the student.

rows: Air-braked vehicles built on or after March 1, 1998; hydraulic-braked trucks and buses of 10,000 lbs GVWR or more built on or after March 1, 1999.
Brake as you normally would. In emergency braking, do not pump the brakes.
Prevents brake-induced wheel lockup so you can keep steering control. It may not shorten stops and does not prevent power or turning skids.

items: Roof-mounted white strobe light: use it when visibility is limited, following state or local rules.
High winds: the bus side acts like a sail. Grip the wheel firmly, slow down or pull off and wait, and contact your dispatcher.
Tail swing can be up to 3 feet. Check mirrors before and during turns.
Backing is strongly discouraged, and never back when students are outside the bus.
Post a lookout to warn you of obstacles, people and vehicles; the lookout should not give backing directions.
With no lookout: set the parking brake, turn off the motor, take the keys, and walk to the rear to check.
Backing at a pick-up point: load students before backing. At a drop-off point: unload after backing.

keyPoints: The danger zone reaches up to 30 feet in front, 10 feet to each side, and 10 feet behind the bus; the left side is always dangerous.
Flat mirrors show 200 feet behind; convex mirrors show the front of the rear tires; crossover mirrors show the front danger zone.
Ambers at least 200 feet before the stop, stop 10 feet from students, then reds when traffic is a safe distance away.
Crossing students walk 10 feet in front of the right bumper corner, stop where you can see their feet, and wait for your signal.
Recognize the hazard first; mandatory evacuations include fire and a bus stalled on or near railroad tracks.
Evacuate to 100 feet off the road toward oncoming traffic, or upwind 300 feet for hazmat.
At railroad crossings, stop 15-50 feet from the nearest rail behind the stop line, and never change gears on the tracks.
Never back up with students outside the bus, and never put a student off except at school or the student's stop.
